mcqs.question: What's the actual cause of a "pattern explosion" that this question is asking you to diagnose?
options: A pattern applied per method instead of per real axis of variation, splitting one underlying concept across several small classes
The codebase simply has too many total lines of code
The team is using more than one programming language
The build system takes too long to compile all the classes
mcqs.explanation: The real cause is structural: patterns get reapplied per method rather than per genuine axis of variation, splitting one concept across many classes. Total line count, multiple languages, and build time aren't what this diagnosis is about.

mcqs.question: How do you tell a real axis of variation from an imagined one when deciding what to consolidate?
options: A real axis is any interface with more than one implementation, regardless of usage
Check whether multiple implementations are actually swapped for each other under different real conditions in production, versus one doing all the real work while another exists just in case
An axis is real only if it was documented in the original design spec
An axis is imagined only if it has exactly one implementation
mcqs.explanation: The real test is whether implementations are genuinely exercised interchangeably in production today — if deleting all but one implementation wouldn't break anything running, the axis was imagined. Interface count alone, original documentation, and implementation count don't determine this on their own.

mcqs.question: What's the recommended way to walk back a pattern explosion in a codebase you didn't design, without a big-bang rewrite?
options: Rewrite the entire module in one large pull request to ensure full consistency
Leave it entirely alone, since consolidating existing code is always too risky to attempt
Consolidate one small cluster at a time, verified via 'find usages' and shipped as its own small, tested commit, before moving to the next cluster
Delete all the classes first, then rebuild functionality from scratch based on memory of what they did
mcqs.explanation: An incremental, cluster-by-cluster approach — verify no outside dependents, consolidate, test, ship independently — avoids the open-ended-rewrite failure mode. A single giant PR, doing nothing at all, or deleting first and rebuilding from memory are all considerably riskier.

mcqs.question: Why is merging several unrelated classes into one "generic" manager class, purely to reduce class count, often the wrong fix for pattern explosion?
options: It's never wrong — reducing class count is always an improvement regardless of what the classes represent
It only fails if the resulting class exceeds 1000 lines of code
It's wrong only when the merged classes are in different packages

If the classes represented genuinely distinct concepts, merging them trades a navigation problem for a new coupling problem, where unrelated concerns now share dependencies and a change to one risks breaking the other
mcqs.explanation: Merging only helps when the classes were truly facets of one concept — otherwise you've just relocated the problem into a new, more tightly coupled form. There's no fixed line-count threshold or package-based rule that determines whether this is safe; what matters is whether the concepts were actually the same to begin with.
